title: Dynam3D: Dynamic Layered 3D Tokens Empower VLM for Vision-and-Language Navi

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.1, Eq. (2), “Updating the Patch Feature Points”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The stated culling rule removes a stored point when it projects inside the current image and satisfies z_c < d_{u,v} + delta. This removes points on the currently observed surface (where z_c is approximately d_{u,v}) while retaining a previously stored point behind a newly observed closer object (where z_c > d_{u,v} + delta). For dynamic-scene replacement, the latter is the stale/occluded point that must be removed. Thus the inequality is opposite to the condition needed to remove prior geometry occluded by new foreground geometry, contradicting the claim that frustum culling discards outdated features after scene changes.

The paper states that Dynam3D achieves “modest improvements of approximately 1-2% in navigation success rate (SR)” over prior state of the art. Table 1 instead reports R2R-CE Val SR of 52.9 for Dynam3D versus the prior best listed SR of 47.2 (g3D-LF) or 47.0 (Uni-NaVid), a 5.7-5.9 percentage-point increase. On Test, 51.4 versus 46.3 is a 5.1-point increase. The prose materially misreports the improvements shown in its own table.

The paper says Dynam3D outperforms NaVid by “approximately 3-5% in Success Rate (SR) on REVERIE-CE and NavRAG-CE.” Table 2 gives REVERIE-CE SR 40.1 for Dynam3D and 26.6 for NaVid, a 13.5-percentage-point difference, not 3-5 points. NavRAG-CE is 24.7 versus 19.4, a 5.3-point difference. The stated range therefore omits and substantially understates the largest reported result.

The text claims that feature dropout and spatial jitter were used to degrade instance/zone embeddings and that performance “degrades significantly more when 3D representation quality is compromised.” However, Table 7 contains only four conditions for SLAM noise and depth noise; it has no feature-dropout or spatial-jitter condition, no values for those ablations, and no statistical test. The asserted comparative degradation is unsupported by the reported evidence.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.6, Table 7 and accompanying robustness protocol
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The depth-noise protocol is not reproducible: it says only that noise is “added with a magnitude proportional to distance,” without a distribution, coefficient, clipping rule, whether it is per-pixel or per-frame, or whether it is applied before projection/segmentation. The claimed feature-dropout and spatial-jitter experiments are also absent from the table. Consequently, neither the reported depth-noise condition nor the claimed representation-quality stress test is sufficiently specified to reproduce.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.2, Table 3 and its interpretation of “pre-exploration” and “lifelong memory”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The pre-exploration protocol explicitly constructs representations of “the entire scene” from panoramic images collected at annotated Matterport3D navigable viewpoints before evaluation. The lifelong-memory protocol then evaluates episodes from the same scene consecutively while retaining those scene representations. These are privileged prior-access and within-test-scene retention settings, rather than ordinary unseen-scene VLN evaluation. The paper itself acknowledges that controls for test-scene familiarity and training overlap are limited and that gains could reflect “environment memorization or data leakage,” yet still presents the results as evidence of lifelong-memory capability. Without scene-disjoint, order-controlled, and no-pre-scan controls, the causal attribution to lifelong memory is not established.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.1/Table 2 and Appendix A.1, baseline retraining
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: For REVERIE-CE and NavRAG-CE, the paper says NaVid and g3D-LF were retrained on “our training dataset” for fairness, but neither Section 4 nor Appendix A.1 specifies the baseline architectures/checkpoints, training schedules, data mixtures, action parameterization, hyperparameters, selection criteria, or whether their original training procedures were retained. Appendix A.1 specifies only Dynam3D training. Because Table 2 depends on newly produced baseline numbers rather than published evaluations, this omission prevents reproduction and assessment of the fairness claim.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, first paragraph; Related Work, “3D Vision-Language Models”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper cites “[8–10]” as “video-language large models” and later includes the same range among “2D-VLM” developments. Reference [10] is Vicuna, described in the bibliography as an open-source chatbot; it is a text-only language model, not a video-language model or a 2D vision-language model. This is a mischaracterization of the cited work.

The claim that a “3.8 billion-parameter LLaVA-Phi-3-mini [52, 53]” is integrated is not supported by the cited references. Reference [52] is XTuner, a fine-tuning toolkit, and reference [53] is the Phi-3 technical report, which documents a language model rather than a LLaVA/Phi-3 multimodal model. Neither reference identifies or documents the asserted LLaVA-Phi-3-mini architecture, visual connector, or 3.8B VLM checkpoint.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.1, “Feature Distillation and Language Alignment for 3D Zones”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Zones are defined as representations obtained by aggregating instances belonging to a fixed spatial cubic zone. But the purported zone-level distillation target is obtained by aggregating all instances “that belong to the same 2D view,” and the paper explicitly concedes that these instances “do not strictly come from the same cube zone.” A view-wide aggregate can span multiple zones and is therefore not a ground-truth representation of the fixed cube zone being supervised. The loss target is misaligned with the stated zone representation and no assignment or aggregation rule is supplied to resolve that mismatch.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.3 and Appendix A.1, real-world dynamic-environment evaluation
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The dynamic experiment is described only as moving the target manually “once the robot approaches,” with 20 test cases and a one-meter stopping criterion. The paper does not specify target classes, instructions, initial robot-target distances, the approach threshold, movement distance/direction/timing, whether the target remains observable, trial randomization, repeated runs, failure handling, or uncertainty estimates. Appendix A.1 supplies hardware and a broad environment description but not these dynamic-test controls. The reported real-world comparison therefore cannot be reproduced or meaningfully separated from operator-dependent intervention.
